World.title: Why Budget Day is a big deal
World.content:
Photo: VNP/Phil Smith

Explainer: It's the most wonderful time of year... if you're a Budget nerd, that is.

Thursday is Budget Day, the biggest day of the year for politicians, other than Election Day.

It's when Finance Minister Nicola Willis will lay out how money will be spent - and what it won't be spent on - for the next fiscal year.

It's a huge event for all the pundits and politicians, but what does it actually all mean?

Here's your primer on what to expect:

What is the Budget?

It's how the government tells us where it's going to spend money and where that money comes from.

Every May, traditionally on a Thursday, the finance minister delivers the Budget in a speech to Parliament. This speech makes a case for how the government plans to spend money and manage the economy.

Read more about this year's Budget:

The primary Budget bill is the Appropriation Bill, which seeks parliamentary authorisation for specific amounts of money for the government in the coming year.

The government must present its Budget to Parliament by 31 July every year.

While everyone talks about Budget 'Day', the process actually carries on all year, cycling perpetually from one Budget to the next.

Select committees go on to scrutinise the spending plans and pass the Budget that was presented on Budget Day.

For example, the 2025/26 Appropriation Bill passed its third reading on 11 September last year, after being introduced in May.

Photo: RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

What happens on Budget Day itself?

Budget Day is equal part numbers-crunching, and political pomp and pageantry.

Everything from how the Budget documents are printed to what kind of snacks politicians might eat beforehand - pies for Sir John Key, cheese scrolls for Dame Jacinda Ardern's government and, last year, Willis presented cookies baked by her daughter - is carefully planned out.

"All Budget statements are a sales pitch, rather than a fair summary," RNZ's The House noted last year.

Here's what happens on the day:

10.30am - Media and other interested parties go into lock-up at the Beehive - no phones, no internet - and get a first look at the Budget. Documents will be released under a strict embargo.

The finance minister will also present to journalists during lock-up and journalists will dash to complete first takes on the highlights. If you break that embargo, you can get in big trouble.

2pm - The Budget embargo lifts and, here at RNZ and everywhere else, you'll suddenly see a flood of Budget information.

Willis will give her Budget Statement to Parliament, laying out the government's plans, kicking off a day of speeches and debate.

"The minister of finance speaks first to make the Budget speech," said a spokesperson for the Clerk of the House of Representatives.

"The minister's speech is then normally followed by the leader of the opposition and then the PM. That isn't cast in stone, but it is what traditionally occurs.

"Once the PM has spoken, it's usual for the leaders of the other political parties to speak in the debate. That is usually in the order of the size of the party in the House."

Parliament will go on to debate the Budget details, which can last up to eight hours.

Of course, RNZ will be there to live-blog coverage throughout the day, and we will have heaps of articles, commentary and reaction to follow up the release.

Photo: VNP / Phil Smith

Why should we care about Budget Day anyway?

Well, it's your money and how it's being spent.

"Because it's the one set-piece that shows us what public services the current government is spending and investing in, and how they will pay for it," Simplicity chief economist and media commentator Shamubeel Eaqub said.

"We have relatively transparent fiscal reporting in New Zealand, meaning we have good insight on what the government is spending on, what it is cutting, and whether it will be paid for by taxes or debt."

Michael Swanson is a research fellow in the University of Otago politics programme.

He said people should care about the Budget, as it shows what the government thinks is important - but it also should show its future plans for the country.

"It gives a snapshot of what the government places value on and allows everyday Kiwis to decide if that aligns with their view on where New Zealand is heading.

"Most of all, Kiwis should ask, 'Does this Budget make my life, and the life of my family and community, better than it was yesterday?'"

Photo: RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

What's this year's message look like?

"There will be no splashing the cash," Willis said, while making the date announcement.

This year's Budget Policy Statement came out in December. Since then, let's just say the world hasn't exactly remained static, as the US/Israel war against Iran has upended the global economy.

Even in December, the message was "New Zealand is in a challenging fiscal position".

"In a more volatile world, we must focus on controlling what we can control and that starts at home," Prime Minister Christopher Luxon told Business NZ recently.

Of course, it's an election year, so the government will try to make the case for another term in November.

"They will do their best to signal their suitability to govern again, while at the same time, leave as little money in future budgets as possible, so the opposition cannot make big promises, without unwinding what is already announced," Eaqub said.

So far, we know that less spending on new programmes will be announced, but spending on capital projects will rise.

The budget operating allowance - the amount of recurring annual funding for new programmes - has been dropped to $2.1 billion. By comparison, in 2022,. then-Finance Minister Grant Robertson set an operating allowance of $5.9b.

However, Willis has proposed an increase in capital expenditure - one-off spending on projects like roads, schools and hospitals - up from $3.5 to $5.7b.

Willis has said the capital spending increase was a result of making investments towards growth.

"We have capital-intensive plans for the future - that includes re-equipping our defence force, it includes ensuring our transport networks are fit for future growth, that we have the hospitals and the schools that we need."

"Budget 2026 is about securing New Zealand's future," Luxon said in pre-Budget remarks. "Fiscal repair, balanced with careful capital investment features heavily in that story.

"The government remains committed to putting debt on a downward path towards 40 percent of GDP and to returning the books to surplus by 2028/29.

"Achieving that will be a tall order and will require careful choices in the years to come."

Swanson said past Budgets had often failed to articulate long-term goals.

"We have a real problem with being future focused and this is something that has hampered consecutive governments.

"What does the country look like in 2030, 2036 or 2040? Rather than just saying, 'We're being fiscally responsible', they need to explain why and what the end goal is."

Eaqub said every Budget had to include difficult choices.

"A surplus is easy to deliver - raise taxes or cut spending - but neither is popular, because each come with winners and losers."

Last time the government was in surplus was in 2019, just before the Covid-19 pandemic.

"We will not balance the books, if we aren't willing to have a proper conversation about what public services we want, of what quality and who pays for it," Eaqub said. "There are no free lunches."

When it comes down to it, with all the speeches on Thursday, the Budget needs to speak clearly to the concerns of ordinary New Zealanders, Swanson said.

"I'd also say that the missing piece is the human element," he said. "The current government have an issue with managing the human impacts of choices made and speak instead in fiscal terms.

"As a result, communication about these decisions comes across as quite defensive, arguing that stability is key to getting through tough times, rather than how this truly makes New Zealand a better place to live.

"What they need to do is show they understand the human impacts of the decisions being made."

World.title: Wahine makes history as first Māori head of School of Nursing
World.content:
Photo: Layla Bailey-McDowell / RNZ

A 17-year-old kōtiro stepping onto a nursing course could never have imagined she would one day become the first Māori head of the School of Nursing at Waipapa Taumata Rau, University of Auckland.

But on Monday morning, surrounded by whānau, colleagues and supporters at Waipapa Marae, Josephine Davis (Ngāti Manu, Ngāti Whātua Ōrākei) was formally welcomed into the historic role.

Davis said the appointment represented an important moment of visibility for future generations of Māori entering nursing and health leadership.

"I want to say to the 17-year-old girl who went on a nursing course, where she was picked up from school and taken to one of the nursing schools to see if this might be the career that she wanted to do, never in her wildest dreams would she have thought she would be standing here today," Davis said following the pōwhiri.

"And so, I hope that for all those tauira Māori out there … they see people that look like them in these spaces."

Davis said she also carried generations of wāhine with her into the role.

"I come from a line of strong wāhine. So, the people who sit on my shoulders on the daily are my grandmothers.

"One of my grandmothers was brought up by her nanny, who was a healer who used to ride around the community on horseback and deliver babies and care for the whānau that were unwell, and I think they're with me every day."

Photo: Layla Bailey-McDowell / RNZ

Davis brings nearly 40 years of experience across nursing practice, education, workforce development and Māori health advocacy. She was also among the country's first Māori nurse practitioners.

Speaking to RNZ after the pōwhiri, Davis said she felt "overwhelmed" but proud to lead the School of Nursing.

"I just really hope that having a Māori leading the school shows really clear visibility and pathway for other Māori who might not necessarily have aspired to these types of roles."

She said visible Māori leadership mattered because rangatahi needed to see different examples of leadership.

"Without visible leaders, people see one type of leadership and that's not the only right type of leadership."

Over the course of her career Davis said she had seen Māori nurses increasingly move into senior leadership positions, rather than remaining solely in frontline clinical roles.

"Our two chief nurses in Aotearoa [are] wāhine Māori, so to have Māori in leadership roles across the sector just shows the potential for our people."

Photo: Layla Bailey-McDowell / RNZ

Davis also reflected on moments early in her career that pushed her toward leadership and further study.

"I can remember clearly working in a particular service and not feeling happy with some of the things that were happening in nursing. And when I looked around the executive leadership table of nursing, there was one Māori, and it was at that time that I decided to start studying again."

She said she had also witnessed significant changes within tertiary institutions themselves.

"At that time, coming to a marae as part of my work would never have been imagined. And so I really feel privileged to have witnessed the transition of the university, of the School of Nursing, and that mātauranga Māori and Māori values are lived and breathed every day, with the people, and the culture."

The appointment came during Budget week and amid ongoing pressure on the country's health workforce, including nursing shortages and wider debates around Māori health equity and Te Tiriti obligations.

Davis said nurses across Aotearoa deserved greater recognition and investment.

"When I talk to my colleagues working out clinically, they are doing amazing work... I just really want them to be seen and acknowledged by our leaders in this country."

She described nursing as critical to healthcare and to the wellbeing of communities.

"We've got 85,000 nurses across Aotearoa across all scopes of practice. We know that nurses, frontline staff, they're the ones that are doing the caring 365 days of the week, 24 hours of the day.

"So they're a workforce that has significant influence, not only in their professional lives, but in their personal lives. They're the ones that often lead the families, that provide that hauora across the families and communities. So I think investment in a nursing workforce isn't just about a profession - it's actually about future-proofing."

Photo: Layla Bailey-McDowell / RNZ

Dean of the Faculty of Medical and Health Sciences, Professor Warwick Bagg, said Davis' appointment represented an important milestone for the university and Māori leadership within health education.

"We've been fortunate in our faculty to have several Māori leaders emerge, and here's another one emerging," he told RNZ.

"She'll be the first in the School of Nursing, the first among many."

Bagg also used the occasion to reflect on what he described as growing challenges around Te Tiriti and Māori health protections.

"Our business is health and health equity," he said. "When we continue to see a real gap for Māori and non-Māori, then we need to have the legislation that protects those rights-led health obligations that we have."

Speaking during the pōwhiri, Bagg referenced recent legislative changes impacting Te Tiriti provisions across multiple sectors, including the proposed repeal of section 7 of the Pae Ora legislation in the Healthy Futures (Pae Ora) Amendment Bill.

"The work is never done," he said. "And my challenge to Josephine and to all of us as we sit here on Monday is the wero has been laid down and we have to pick it up again.

"We will not be quiet."

Photo: Layla Bailey-McDowell / RNZ

Despite the challenges facing the sector, Davis said nursing remained an incredibly rewarding career and hoped rangatahi Māori feel inspired to enter the profession.

"Never has my nursing career been easy, but it has always been rewarding," she said.

"You can't underestimate the value of holding someone's hand in their darkest days, being there to witness the birth of children, being there to awhi someone when their loved one passes away. That's all nurses."

World.title: Gulf Harbour body trial: Rice bags around body led to the accused
World.content:
Photo: RNZ / Marika Khabazi

The Chinese woman whose body was found in Auckland's Gulf Harbour came to seek religious instruction from Kaixiao Liu, one of the people accused of killing her, the Crown says.

Shulai Wang, 70, came to New Zealand in 2023 from China's Hainan province and her body was found wrapped in plastic bags floating in water in March 2024.

Four family members have been accused of the kidnapping and manslaughter of Wang, and are facing trial in the Auckland High Court.

They were Liu and his wife Lanyue Xiao, both 38, as well as Liu's mother Xiuyun Li, 63, and Liu's father Jingui Liu, 65.

Crown prosecutor Emma Kerr said Wang had suffered blunt force injuries on her head, face and arms, and was denied food and locked up in a tent before her death.

She said it was believed that Wang was punished as she was believed to be breaking the rules of Liu's house, where she stayed.

Photo: RNZ / Marika Khabazi

The rice bags

Police were called when fisherman Paul Middleton found a hand sticking out of the plastic bags on 12 March 2024.

Kerr said a human body bent in half at the waist and bound with black tape in the foetal position was found when the bags were unwrapped at the Auckland City Hospital mortuary the next day.

The two plastic rice bags contained garden stones used to weigh the body down, and proved to be key in how officers found the accused, Kerr said in her opening statement.

"Taking the serial number of each of those rice bags, police managed to work out some potential locations as to where they might have been brought," she said.

Officers found someone purchased an unusually large amount of the rice - 15 bags of the 10-kilogram rice - at a North Shore supermarket and traced the bank account to Liu.

The bank account also led police to one of Liu's fuel purchases, and CCTV footage of him getting petrol for a white Mercedes van.

Kerr said the same van was seen on CCTV footage at the Gulf Harbour Marina - days before Wang's body was discovered - showing five people "including children" walking between the van and the floodgate bridge leading to the ocean.

The footage showed the individuals were pulling an item believed to be a pram containing Wang's wrapped body, said Kerr.

Photo: RNZ / Marika Khabazi

'The Ark' - a house on Orewa's Harvest Avenue

Apart from the four family members, police found Liu and Xiao's four young children when they visited Liu's house in Orewa, as well as five other women staying in the house, which was referred to as the "Ark".

As the leader of the religious group, Liu was referred to the "Lord", and his wife Xiao was referred to as the "Queen", while the unrelated women lived in servitude to Liu and his family.

Kerr did not elaborate on what rules Wang might have broken, but said Wang was locked up in a tent on the deck of the house and deprived of food.

She tried to escape to the neighbour's property, but was caught and taken back, her body bound in tape and her mouth taped over to stop her from screaming, Kerr said.

Wang and her family were among the more than 30 families following Liu, Kerr said.

Diaries and recordings found in the house detailed how Wang was treated before her death, as well as discussions around how to explain Wang's death.

Kerr said records showed Kaixiao Liu and his father exchanging ideas on how to tie up Wang, and Liu saying, "Shulai's case is a result of long-term listening to the dark side of the inner world, and not listening to God's way."

She said in some of the recordings, Ms Wang was characterised in Liu's teachings as "evil" and that he spoke of the threat she posed to "God's family".

Kaixiao Liu: 'We want to find out the truth'

Given an opportunity to respond to the Crown's opening, Kaixiao Liu said "we want to find out the truth".

"All the information about the elderly were hearsay from other ladies who took care of her. I did have some communication with those ladies, I question them and encouraged them in difficult times, I want them to tell me the truth but everyone gave me different answers," he said.

Liu said he "almost" had no contact with the "elderly".

He also requested the court to call nine key witnesses - the five other women and four children.

Liu's wife Xiao told the jury the Crown had given their "assumptions" and she wanted the jury to carefully examine whether their narrative was supported by evidence.

"Whether there are possibility to misinterpret these diaries or recordings to support their narrative," she told a jury of six men and six women.

Photo: Supplied / Police

Paul Middleton, the fisherman who found Wang's body, and another witness who noticed the bag while walking his dog also gave evidence in court.

The four defendants, accompanied by Mandarin interpreters, chose to represent themselves with stand-by lawyers being assigned to each of them.

They urged the jury to keep an open mind and thanked the jury for their services.

Earlier in the day, the court granted the Crown prosecutor's application to remove allegation of assault in relation to the alleged manslaughter.

Liu, his mother and Xiao have also been charged with improperly interfering with or offering an indignity to a dead human body.

Liu and his wife were charged with attempt to pervert course of justice by coaching Wang's son to give false evidence regarding his mother.

Liu also faced another charge of failing to carry out obligations in relation to computer system search when requested by the police.

Justice Mathew Downs said the trial could last four to six weeks.

World.title: Surfing: Carissa Moore and Italo Ferreira win New Zealand Pro at Raglan
World.content:
Photo: Rambo Estrada

World champions and Olympic gold medalists Carissa Moore and Italo Ferreira won the New Zealand Pro at Raglan, both claiming their first victories since becoming parents.

Hawaii's Moore won her first Championship Tour event since 2023, after two seasons away welcoming her daughter, 'Olena, to the world.

Moore defeated Sawyer Lindblad of the United States in the final in the best conditions of the event at Manu Bay.

After Lindblad struck first for a small score, Moore took the second exchange, opening with an excellent 8.50 over a 7.67 from Lindblad.

A fall from Moore on a larger set wave opened the door for Lindblad to take the upper hand. The Southern Californian goofy-footer drove through a series of searing forehand carves to post a 9.00, leaving Moore in need of an 8.18.

Photo: Rambo Estrada/WSL

The Hawaiian continued to attack but was unable to find excellence again until the six-minute mark, when a steep inside section opened up for her to seamlessly deliver a combination of three powerful backhand blasts and earn a 9.40, for a 17.90 heat total.

"I was on the ropes for a good portion of that heat. When [Sawyer Lindblad] dropped that 9.00, I was like, OK, well, I need a wave and I need to show up," Moore said.

"Sawyer's been on point all event. I respect her so much and I think she's really found her form this year."

The five-time world champion dominated the first Championship Tour (CT) event to be held at New Zealand's premier left point, posting the highest heat totals in every round, including the overall highest of the season in the semi-finals, a near-perfect 19.00 (out of a possible 20).

The result further solidifies Moore's place at No. 2 on the all-time CT win list with 29 victories.

Photo: Oscar Hetherington/World Surf League

Moore also won the first women's CT to be held in New Zealand, at Taranaki in 2010. It was her first victory as a 17-year-old Rookie on Tour and she gifted all her prize money to the local Waitara Bar Boardriders Club, a contingent of which came to support her in this event.

"This place has held a special place in my heart for a really long time. My experience here in 2010 changed my whole perspective on my career, what success looked like and how I wanted to live.

"I just want to say a big mahalo to the community in Taranaki but also here, and how you all have shown up every single day. The love and the energy and the mana in this place are indescribable and something I will remember for the rest of my life."

Having won the regular season for every year she has competed on the CT since 2019, the 33-year-old's move to No. 6 on the season rankings is a major threat to the new generation on tour.

"This is for the mums - never stop dreaming if you want to," Moore said.

"When I walked away two years ago, I didn't know if I'd ever get this feeling back or this opportunity to surf perfect waves with only one other person out in front of a beautiful crowd and at a beautiful place with my family on the beach.

"In that process, you doubt yourself so much, and so I think the win means so much to me.

"I do want to say thank you to my husband because without him this wouldn't be possible. To my beautiful daughter, who is adapting to all these conditions and places we're going, I couldn't do it if she weren't willing to; she has given me a strength that I didn't even know I had."

Photo: www.photosport.nz

Italo Ferreira reclaimed the No. 1 position on the rankings following his 11th CT win and will wear the Yellow Leader Jersey headed into the Surf City El Salvador Pro for the second year in a row.

Also a new parent, Ferreira is feeling a fresh drive on tour as he competes for his son and wife.

"I'm so stoked to win a comp on a left, like a real left, because in the past we've had Teahupo'o, Pipe - some big ones but not a perfect one," Ferreira said.

"I was like, OK, this can be my comp, because I've been surfing so much, dedicating a lot. I've been on the road for two months without my kid, without my wife. I was like, OK, it's time to put all the energy into this event. I just want to say thank you to God for everything. The opportunity to stay here, to be here, to win this comp, to have a great family, to have a beautiful history behind me, and I'm still going. That's my energy. I'm creating a new life right now, and it's been so sick. Dad's power, right? I'm so happy."

The Final saw two of the event standouts, with totally contrasting styles: the super-fast, electric frontside surfing of Ferreira up against the rock-solid, critical backside snaps of Morgan Cibilic from Australia.

Both competitors brought their A-game to the heat, each posting their highest two-wave total of the entire event in the 40-minute matchup.

Cibilic took an early advantage, smashing a series of massive vertical re-entries to earn an 8.90 and put Ferreira on the ropes.

Ferreira looked unfazed, returning serve with 9.33 for back-to-back air-reverses on the one wave, followed by a number of carves and snaps down the line.

As the ocean slowed, Cibilic missed the last wave he could have surfed in the heat, leaving Ferreira to claim his first win in over 12 months.

"This has been an amazing event," Ferreira said.

"We have been waiting for this left, and even once we got here to New Zealand, we had to wait a little longer than the last two days it came to life. Getting to show a different type of surfing than we usually do on all of the rights has been so good and so much fun. I've really loved this place and had an amazing time surfing here and hanging out with my crew. I can't wait to come back. It was good in the Final hearing, all of the support for us, and well done to Morgan, he was surfing all week amazingly."

World.title: More than 30 faith leaders, clergy pen open letter criticising bill to move on rough sleepers
World.content:
Photo: RNZ / Nick Monro

More than 30 Auckland faith leaders and clergy have put put their names to an open letter criticising the government's bill to move on rough sleepers.

The legislation passed its first reading on Thursday following a heated debate at Parliament.

The Summary Offences (Move-on Orders) Amendment Bill would give police the power to issue move-on orders to people who are displaying disorderly, disruptive, threatening, or intimidating behaviour.

They will also apply to people who are obstructing or impeding someone entering a business, breaching the peace, begging, rough sleeping, or displaying behaviour indicating an attempt to inhabit a public place.

After being issued with such an order, the person has to leave a specified order for up to 24 hours, and what the officer deems to be a "reasonable distance" away.

People as young as 14 would be subject to the orders.

An open letter, signed by 31 clergy in Auckland, urged the government to provide more funding for homelessness support programmes.

"We believe that the way to solve the growing problem of rough sleeping in our cities is not to move people on. It is to provide stable accommodation and appropriate wrap-around support services," the letter said.

"While there may be instances when anti-social behaviour needs to be responded to, moving a person on to an unspecified place will do nothing to address the issues they are dealing with. In many cases, moving rough sleepers on may cause harm, disconnecting them from friends, support services, and ironically, regular police supervision.

"If this policy is not accompanied by significant increases in support for Housing First programmes and transitional housing, then we are not solving the problem of rough sleeping."

Inner-city priest Reverend Cate Thorn from St Matthew-in-the-City said the policy had the potential to cause real harm to vulnerable people.

"The bill isn't going to work. The government's restricted emergency housing, selling off state houses, recently restricted access to social housing. Homelessness has increased in the last couple of years. The bill doesn't solve homelessness, it just moves the issue around the city," she said.

"There's an increasing population of people, for example women in the 65 plus age group, people who just simply can't afford housing, who are having no choice but to move. And so within Auckland itself there is an increasing number of people who are living without houses and in the cold weather that's not getting any better."

Thorn told Checkpoint the government should be working for those vulnerable people, not against them.

"The intention of this letter is to make it very public those of us who align ourselves with some sort of faith community are naming the harm that can be done to the vulnerable people in our communities, and to indicate the move-on orders are not creating any solutions for those who are made homeless," she said.

"We as a community have a responsibility to address the real issues, not just to make the inconvenient disappear periodically.

"I think some of the current policymaking seems to be focused on profit lines and economics rather than the reality of people," she said.

Speaking at the first reading on Thursday, Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith said the bill was not criminalising homelessness, but would simply give police the power to issue move-on orders.

Only people who refused to follow the orders would face prosecution, and people lawfully protesting or conducting charitable or not-for-profit fundraising would be exempt.

Goldsmith said there had been "unprecedented" levels of disruption in city centres with businesses, residents, and visitors playing the price.

"Our focus is ensuring that we reclaim those streets and those town centres for the enjoyment of people who live there, who work there, who visit there," he said.

World.title: When dogs fly: Re-homed greyhounds could be flown to Australia
World.content:
Photo: PHOTOSPORT

A charter plane could fly dozens of greyhounds to Australia to avoid a dog racing ban in New Zealand.

Greyhound racing will be illegal in Aotearoa from August.

The move follows several critical reviews of the industry and concerns around animal welfare.

A Greyhound Transition Agency has been set up to help re-home up to 2000 dogs and was responsible for their welfare until then.

But Greyhound Racing NZ is floating the idea of taking up to 70 dogs on a charter flight to Queensland - where racing was still legal.

Chief executive Edward Rennell told Checkpoint this could help some trainers reduce some of the losses they were incurring.

"We believe some individuals might want to send some dogs to Australia, we're not talking about sending every dog in their kennel, but there may be a trainer looking to send two or three and then you add who would be competitive in Australia and a chance for them to minimize some of the expenses they've incurred," he said.

"We're looking to see whether collectively there's enough interest to justify a charter flight. There's no guarantee it will happen unless we can make it viable up around the 60 or 70 number but that's still a minor number of the 1700 that will need to be re-homed post 1 August," he said.

Rennell said trainers would likely race the dogs in Australia.

"There would be only the very top dogs that would be competitive, no different to the top thoroughbred and harness horses who go over to Australia and race. There may be some of the very well bred dogs that may be sent over there for breeding purposes but you're really talking the top dogs that it would be viable for them to do that," he said.

Rennell said Greyhound Racing New Zealand would cover the cost of the charter if it got off the ground.

The industry and the Greyhound Transition Agency had been at loggerheads over payments to keep caring for the greyhounds until they were effectively adopted out.

The agency told RNZ it was not aware of the charter plane proposal.

It said the budget for the transition agency had now been set, the contract was in development and it would advise the industry of next steps this week, including advice of the daily rates.

It did not expect any extension for the deadline for the end of greyhound racing in New Zealand.

World.title: Global tax cheats with a Kiwi enabler
World.content:
Photo: James O'Brien/OCCRP

The big story of a tiny New Zealand company that's made front page news on a website exposing international organised crime and corruption.

An international collaboration and months of forensic investigation and fact-checking has helped a small Kiwi financial journalism website break a story involving a New Zealand company that moved massive amounts of money for multiple clients who were later convicted of financial crimes.

Worldclear Limited - a banking clearing house based in Hamilton which is no longer operating - was able to set up and trade without breaking any rules, and it denies it knew anything about what its more colourful clients were up to.

Those clients included a politically connected Belarusian oligarch, a UK citizen convicted as part of a large-scale European tax swindle, a Canadian-American guilty of wire fraud, and a Swedish national for whom there is still an international Red Notice out.

The resulting story features this week on the front page of the website of the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project, a global network of journalists rooting out stories of bribery, coercion and dirty deals in all corners of the globe.

It was written by Gareth Vaughan, the editor of interest.co.nz, but he says he had a lot of help - from journalists from countries including Belarus, Lithuania, Sweden and Singapore.

He has been following the Worldclear story for 10 years, but this investigation was really sparked in 2024 by a leak from a former employee who had been jailed in Singapore for financial crimes.

"I sort of started looking at it and I just realised, there's a lot here," he says.

"This is about events that happened a few years ago ... it's undoubtedly going to be interesting. I had no idea of the scale of it. I didn't realise the business had been anywhere near as big as it actually was in terms of the volumes ... we're talking tens of millions of dollars and various currencies, and customers literally from every corner of the world."

Interest.co.nz applied for a Brian Gaynor Business Journalism Initiative grant and got more than $76,000 to hire temporary cover so that Vaughn could spend time pursuing the story.

Worldclear's business model was to make international banking transactions for customers who were having difficulty doing that, either because banks turned them down or they were from jurisdictions that reputable banks wouldn't deal with. Under anti-money laundering rules it was classed as a remittance company.

It targeted high risk clients facing banking or payment problems - the company says that is not evidence of knowing about or facilitating crimes, and there is no evidence that was the case.

Using firms like Worldclear is a slow and expensive way to transfer money, but it makes transactions harder to track.

It was not a bank so did not have to comply with Reserve Bank standards, and didn't break any rules under what are widely held to be 'light touch' financial regulations in New Zealand - regulations that have the World Bank classing the country as the easiest in the world to do business.

"It's very attractive for business people, right, so anyone who wants to set up a company. [For] legitimate business, it's fantastic, it's great, and it's brilliant.

"But it does mean that there may be people out there whose reasoning may not be completely wholesome - it's easy for them to do as well.

"So Worldclear registered as a New Zealand company, and then it registered as a New Zealand Financial Service Provider. And registering as a Financial Service Provider doesn't mean that you're actually regulated - that's a separate issue. So there are some areas where you can register as a New Zealand Financial Service Provider and provide certain financial services internationally, and you're not actually regulated in New Zealand.

"They didn't do anything wrong in the way they set the company up at all. They followed all the rules. And you can effectively operate as a bank internationally but you're obviously not licenced by the Reserve Bank.

"By international standards this is quite light-touch."

Two of the company's shareholders had financial criminal records, but Worldclear had no obligation to dig into their backgrounds.

"You could set up in the same way today, as Worldclear did," says Vaughan.

"There may be closer oversight of you today... also one of our experts we spoke to said he just didn't think banks would take on a company like this today."

The Department of Internal Affairs, which had oversight of such financial companies, did two inspections and was quite biting about the company's methods in the second one - but no charges were ever laid. By the time that report came out, Worldclear had in 2019 left the Financial Service Provider's register.

It is still a registered company but it has not filed an annual return since 2024 and the Companies Registrar has started the process of de-registering it. Inland Revenue has opposed the company's deregistration.

World.title: Blues send out SOS as playmaker struggles with injury
World.content:
Mitchell Moses is in doubt for the State of Origin opener as the New South Wales playmaker struggled with a hamstring issue, paving the way for a potential debut for Ethan Strange.

Five-eighth Moses trained with the Blues in Gosford today but will be sent for scans by NSW staff after complaining of tightness.

Laurie Daley's men relocated to Sydney today after completing an opposed session against Newcastle's NSW Cup team on the Central Coast.

The anticipated absence of Moses has led to NSW rushing Canterbury five-eighth Matt Burton into camp ahead of Wednesday night's game at Homebush in Sydney.

"The NSW Blues, subject to ARLC (Australian Rugby League Commission) approval, will call Matt Burton into the 20-player squad as stand-by for five-eighth Mitchell Moses, who pulled up with hamstring tightness at the end of training at Polytec Stadium in Gosford," the Blues said in a statement this afternoon.

Matt Burton has been 18th man for NSW in five of its past nine Origin games. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"Moses completed the team session but felt tightness as part of extra activities post the team session, and will undergo scans tomorrow to determine the extent of the injury.

"Subject to ARLC approval, Burton will join camp this evening and train with the team in their final session tomorrow ahead of game one."

Canberra youngster Strange, who was initially named on the Blues interchange, is likely to take the number six jersey alongside halfback Nathan Cleary if Moses cannot line up.

Strange, 21, has yet to play Origin but was part of the Kangaroos tour to England over the off-season.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Legendary former Blues coach Phil Gould and NSW great Andrew Johns have praised Strange's form over the last 18 months, including his key role in Canberra's run to last year's minor premiership.

Strange has 19 tries in 55 NRL games and played for NSW in the 2023 U19 State of Origin game, where he scored a hat-trick.

If Strange is named to make his debut and Burton sits on the bench without getting game time, it could mark the sixth time in the past 10 Origin games that Burton has remained on stand-by.

The former Penrith centre played two Origins in 2022 but has not added to that tally despite repeatedly being named 18th man.

World.title: Neale Daniher to be remembered with state funeral, premier reveals
World.content:
From his playing days through coaching, administration, executive roles and tireless campaigning, Neale Daniher was a prominent figure in Australian Rules football for almost half a century.

Daniher has died after an extraordinary 13-year battle with motor neurone disease (MND), during which he also dedicated himself to raising awareness and funds in search of a cure for the condition.

Daniher's family said he was "a fighter" from day one and took on MND "with everything he had".

Former AFL player and MND campaigner Neale Daniher dies Former Essendon player and Demons coach Neale Daniher has died. He was diagnosed with motor neurone disease in 2013 and campaigned to raise awareness of the disease and increase research.

"Even in the toughest times, he kept pushing forward, determined to land as many blows as he could against his toughest opponent, all with a cheeky grin and a sharp sense of humour that never left him," a statement from the family said.

Having touched so many in his 65 years, Daniher will be honoured with a state funeral service, Victorian Premier Jacinta Allan revealed.

"The family have accepted that offer of a state funeral and arrangements will follow," she said.

"Right now, my thoughts and love go to Jan and the family, and I know the thoughts and love of all Victorians will be going to the Daniher family as we hold them in our hearts today."

Allan said Daniher would not only be remembered for his "incredible contribution" to AFL, but also for his determination to find a cure for MND.

Loading...

"That has touched the lives of so, so many families around the nation, as was recognised during his Australian of the Year recognition," she said.

"We're with [Neale's family] right now, and we'll continue to be with [them] as we keep up Neale's fight against 'the beast' and find a cure for MND."

Neale Daniher with daughter Bec at the Big Freeze fundraiser. (Getty Images: Dylan Burns/AFL Photos)

Daniher's death came just two weeks before the King's Birthday AFL clash between Collingwood and Melbourne, which will play host to the 12th annual Big Freeze fundraiser for FightMND.

It is also less than a week after 30-year-old NRL star Jai Arrow revealed he was diagnosed with MND late last year.

MND has been called 'the beast'. We still don't know what causes it As another footballer is diagnosed with motor neurone disease, we asked experts why so little is known about what causes it.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Daniher in 2025 might have been the most widely supported Australian of the Year winner ever.

"[It was] richly deserved recognition that Neale embraced, not as an accolade but as a platform, a way to continue his advocacy for a cure," he said.

"Neale Daniher's remarkable legacy lives all around us.

"The difference he made can be measured in the national awareness and the tens of millions of dollars that he and FightMND have raised to research a cure."

A legacy across and outside footy

Daniher's death comes just two weeks before the 12th annual Big Freeze fundraiser for Fight MND. (Getty Images: Adam Trafford/AFL Photos)

AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon said Daniher's death was "a devastating loss".

"Not only for everyone fortunate enough to know him, but for everyone in our community for the selflessness that he represented," he said.

Daniher played alongside brothers Terry, Anthony and Chris with the Bombers during his 12 seasons at the club and Neale was named one of the club's Hall of Fame Legends in 2022.

Neale Daniher (second from right), his three brothers and his nephew, Joe, played at Essendon. (Getty Images: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

"Neale will forever be a beloved Bomber and is one of the most remarkable people our game has ever produced," club president Andrew Welsh said.

After his playing career finished in the early 90s, Daniher was one of Fremantle's inaugural assistant coaches from 1995 to 1997 before taking over as coach of the Melbourne Demons in 1998.

Melbourne's longest-serving captain, David Neitz, said Daniher's legacy would be felt across the world.

"The bloody beast has won this battle today but the battle's going to continue on," he said.

" I know that we and all Australians will get behind Neale still and rally for him in a really sad time, but as a mate, it's a really hard thing to take. "

Loading Instagram content

Daniher took the Dees to the 2000 grand final against the Bombers, where they fell short of their first premiership since 1964.

Melbourne Football Club president Steven Smith said it was "impossible to encapsulate" Daniher's impact.

"His courage transcended the football field, and his determination inspired an entire country.

"Neale was not driven by personal motivation, he was driven by helping others, right until the very end.

"He was a true leader and the definition of what it means to be selfless.

Daniher (right) led the Demons to the 2000 AFL grand final. (Getty Images: Hamish Blair/ALLSPORT)

"Neale was a man of action not words, and he embodied the saying, that he himself made famous, 'The mark of a person is not what you say, but what you do.'

"He will be greatly missed by us all, but he will never be forgotten."

After stepping away from the Demons in 2007, Daniher became the chief executive of the AFL Coaches' Association and took up a role as football manager with the West Coast Eagles the following year.

In 2013, Daniher stepped away from the game due to health reasons, revealing the next year that he had been diagnosed with MND.

He dedicated the rest of his life to fighting "the beast", not just for himself but for anyone else diagnosed, becoming the face of the first Big Freeze and raising millions for charity.

MND Australia chief executive Clare Sullivan said the community was "deeply saddened" to hear about the death of one of their "champion fighters".

"The average survival time after diagnosis is 2.5 years … Neale defied those odds and continued to fight and raise awareness of MND," she said.

"In the wake of Neale's passing, Australia must continue to raise awareness for the MND community and advocate for better care, better support services, and continued investment into finding a cure."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Daniher's family said his biggest hope was that people would continue to push on and still crack a smile even when times were at their toughest.

"He wanted to leave a legacy that says this: 'No matter the odds, no matter the diagnosis, we all have the power to fight, to smile, and to do'," the Danihers said.

"Because the mark of a person isn't what they say, 'it's what they do'.

"We will forever remember him for the lasting impact that he has made on us all. He has inspired, he has loved, he has lived and it would only be fitting to finish with his words — Play On."

World.title: V'landys to take over as NRL CEO after Abdo quits to join Tennis Australia
World.content:
NRL chief executive Andrew Abdo has announced his shock mid-season resignation to lead Tennis Australia (TA).

TA had been on the lookout for a new chief executive after Craig Tiley announced in February that he was stepping down this year to become head of the US Tennis Association.

Abdo's resignation comes as the NRL stands on the cusp of unprecedented expansion, welcoming teams in Perth and PNG in 2027 and 2028, respectively.

Abdo will stay with the NRL until July 15 to help complete broadcast negotiations, with Australian Rugby League Commission chair Peter V'landys replacing Abdo until a new CEO is in place.

Andrew Abdo (left) and Peter V'landys (right) have worked together closely for seven years. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"Leading the NRL has been a privilege and the highlight of my career," Abdo said.

"Together we have built a strong, innovative and resilient organisation, expanded the reach of the game and positioned it for an exciting future.

"Rugby league has given me opportunities I could only have dreamed of, experiences that cannot be compared and I have made friendships for a lifetime. It has been an honour to be part of the rugby league family.

"The NRL is in a strong position — strategically, commercially and in how it is governed.

"The game doesn't stand still, and it shouldn't. The game means so much to so many and the future of rugby league has never been more exciting. I look forward to watching that continued success from the outside."

A collective bargaining agreement with the Rugby League Players' Association is up for renewal after the 2027 NRL season.

Abdo took charge of the NRL in April 2020 and helped the league navigate the competition's COVID-enforced shutdown and subsequent resumption that May.

Under Abdo's leadership, the NRL has executed its daring plan to open the season with matches in Las Vegas, a deal that also runs out after 2027.

The league has introduced major changes to its rule-book on Abdo's watch, most notably introducing the divisive set-restart rule.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Abdo was also chief executive when the NRL expanded for the first time since 2007, introducing the Dolphins for the 2023 season.

Prior to replacing Todd Greenberg as chief executive, Abdo had served as the NRL's chief commercial officer from 2013 until 2020, and previously worked in the corporate sector.

Tiley had worked at TA since starting as the player development chief in 2005.

He became the Australian Open tournament director the following year and CEO in 2013 and had been easily Australia's highest-paid sports administrator with a multi-million-dollar salary.

Most of the movers and shakers in Australian tennis are in Paris for the French Open, which started on Sunday.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Breaking: Neale Daniher, former AFL player and motor neurone disease campaigner, dies
World.content:
Former AFL footballer, Australian of the Year and motor neurone disease campaigner Neale Daniher has died at the age of 65.

His family confirmed his death today.

"We're heartbroken to share that our much-loved husband, Dad and Poppy, Neale Daniher, passed away at home, surrounded by his family," the family said in a statement.

"We will forever remember him for the lasting impact that he has made on us all. He has inspired, he has loved, he has lived, and it would only be fitting to finish with his words — Play On."

Daniher played 82 games for Essendon over 11 years of an injury-plagued AFL/VFL career from 1979 to 1990.

He also coached Melbourne Football Club for more than 220 games from 1998 to 2007.

He was diagnosed with motor neurone disease (MND) in 2013 and dedicated his later years to raising awareness of the disease and fundraising for research.

Daniher was named Victorian of the Year in 2019 and Australian of the Year in 2025.

Neale Daniher during his Essendon years. (Supplied)

A family of footy players

Daniher was born in West Wyalong, in New South Wales, in 1961 and played Australian rules football, rugby union and rugby league as a schoolboy.

His older brother, Terry Daniher, one of four Daniher brothers who would play in the AFL or VFL, was already contracted to Essendon when Neale joined the club in 1979.

Daniher showed signs of being a star in the making, playing 23 games as a halfback flanker and kicking nine goals in his first season with the Bombers.

He was named the league's Recruit of the Year and appeared destined for stardom in the game.

He was again a fixture in the side in the 1980 and 1981 seasons, earning a place in the New South Wales representative side and winning Essendon's Best and Fairest in 1981.

The Big Footy: A tiny town's tribute to its AFL giants The NSW town of Ungarie honours Aussie Rules legends Terry, Neale, Anthony and Chris Daniher by unveiling a giant football.

A promising career cut short by injury

At the end of the 1981 season, Daniher suffered a knee injury he thought was minor until doctors revealed he had ruptured a cruciate ligament and would require a full knee reconstruction.

His selection as club captain ahead of the 1982 season was historic for two reasons: he was the youngest player ever picked in the role, and he would also become the only club captain never to lead his team onto the field.

Daniher's knee injury turned out to be even worse than the club had feared, and he spent the next three years on the sidelines before making his comeback in 1985.

Neale Daniher and three of his brothers played at Essendon at the same time in the early 1980s. (Supplied)

However, just five games into the season, he seriously injured his knee again, requiring another reconstruction.

A second comeback in 1987 ended the same way, with Daniher going under the surgeon's knife for a third time.

Daniher handled each injury setback in typical fashion, dealing with the disappointment quickly and quietly before applying himself to getting back on the field.

Speaking to the ABC's Drew Morphett ahead of his comeback game in 1985, he said he would have given the game away if it were not for the support and encouragement of his brothers.

He played just a handful of games in the league's top tier in his final season in 1990, but one of them happened to be in an Essendon side that included his three football-playing siblings.

Daniher named top Victorian AFL great Neale Daniher is named the 2019 Victorian of the Year in recognition of his advocacy to find a cure for the fatal motor neurone disease he was diagnosed with six years ago.

He stopped short of saying the four had a telepathic connection on the field, but admitted they weren't just regular teammates.

"You don't tend to look out for each other, you just have a sense of where your brothers are," he told Andrew Denton on the ABC's Live and Sweaty program in 1991.

"I remember last year we played against St Kilda and I'd been struggling in the reserves and I got a game and they all looked after me pretty well that day."

Daniher makes his mark as a coach

Daniher's on-field career may have been curtailed by injury, but he showed he had plenty to offer on the sidelines, first as an assistant coach at Essendon and Fremantle, then as a senior coach at Melbourne.

In his third season as coach at the Demons, he steered the side to the AFL Grand Final against his old club Essendon, losing the decider by 60 points.

Daniher earned the nickname "The Reverend" during the 2004 season for his attempts to boost the club's profile and membership by "preaching" to supporters to get behind the team.

Neale Daniher addresses his players in 2006. (Getty: Sean Garnsworthy)

His spell as Demons coach ended in 2007 without an AFL premiership, but with the respect of football fans across the country.

He spent five years as general manager of football operations at West Coast before standing down for health reasons that were not publicly known at that time.

Battling 'the beast' after a shock diagnosis

In August 2014, Daniher revealed he had been diagnosed with MND, a disease he referred to as "the beast".

"I call it the beast, mainly because I can personalise it. If I'm going to battle something, I like to give it a name," He told ABC News Breakfast in 2015.

" It's a beast of a disease because it's got a 100 per cent strike rate. Once you're diagnosed, you will die. "

Daniher established the Big Freeze fundraising event for Motor Neurone Disease, which has run for a number of years. (AAP: Tracey Nearmy)

When he publicly revealed his diagnosis, Daniher said MND was a disease that was not very well known, but he made it his task to change that situation, founding the charity Fight MND, which raises money for research.

One of the charity's signature events is the Big Freeze event, which sees celebrities sent hurtling down a slide into freezing water in the middle of the Victorian winter.

The 2024 event raised more than $20 million for MND research.

Daniher told the ABC in 2015 he was certain a cure for MND would be found.

"I always believe if there's a will, there's a way. We're smart. Human beings have got an answer to this, but at the moment, it's hidden away."

Neale Daniher during a Lap of Honour in 2025. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

Speaking at the launch of his autobiography, When All Is Said and Done, in 2019, Daniher said he wanted to leave his grandchildren with some words of wisdom in case he was not able to deliver them in person.

"Life's not about finding yourself, it's about creating yourself. I might not be around, but I'd like to leave a few signposts for them," he said.

"I hope my kids understand that life doesn't promise to be fair. It will be hard. It will be tough. You might have setbacks, but life is generally good if you understand it won't be fair and if you know that, you can go about life looking for opportunities.

"Find opportunities when you suffer, and it gives you opportunities to grow towards the better side of your nature."

Neale Daniher, wife Jan and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese during the 2025 Australian of the Year Awards. (AAP: Mick Tsikas)

By the time Daniher was named Australian of the Year in January 2025, he was unable to speak, so a prerecorded audio version of his remarks was played at the ceremony.

"I chose to fight because if I didn't, how could I expect anyone else to? I chose to hope because I believe in the decency and generosity of Australians," he said.

"I thought, if people truly understood the challenges we face, and joined the fight with me — and you have, oh, how you have.

"To everyone who has bought a beanie, donated a dollar, or spread the word — thank you. You are proof that when Australians unite, nothing is impossible."

He is survived by his wife, Jan, and their four children and multiple grandchildren.

World.title: Gold medallist who endured 16 surgeries in 9 months hangs up oars
World.content:
Nikki Ayers endured 16 surgeries in the space of nine months on her way to the top of the podium at the Paralympics, but there are some challenges the gold medal-winning rower has struggled to face as she looks back over an amazing career.

The 35-year-old took up para-rowing following a devastating rugby union injury which left her with permanent damage to her peroneal nerve and popliteal artery causing her to develop foot drop.

She also developed compartment syndrome from a lack of blood supply to the lower part of her right leg, which led to a series of surgeries to remove dead muscle tissue.

"I thought my whole sporting career was taken away from me and I lost that identity," Ayers said.

" Rowing was that light at the end of the tunnel. "

Teaming up with Jed Altschwager, Ayers claimed Australia's first para-rowing gold medal at the 2024 Paralympics, winning the PR3 Mixed Double Scull.

Nikki Ayers and Jed Altschwager winning gold in 2024. (Supplied: AAP Image/Jeff Crow, via Sport the Library/Paralympics Australia)

Although she reached the pinnacle of that sport, the para-rower recently spoke out about facing ableism, homophobia and sexism throughout her career.

Announcing her retirement, Ayers said she hoped athletes in the future would be given more support and "psychological safety" if facing discrimination.

"I hope they don't have to face the challenges that are purely related to being female," she said.

"I want there to be systemic changes so athletes have a voice … so they can speak up and are believed."

Nikki Ayers has undergone 16 surgeries on her right leg after an injury during a rugby union match. (ABC News: Tony Hill)

Ayers took time off from rowing earlier this year and also pulled back on her work in healthcare.

Taking a step back helped her realise that retirement from rowing was the right decision.

"Rowing at the elite level and shift work as a nurse and midwife takes over your life," Ayers said.

"It just didn't feel right going back to rowing."

" It just felt like I needed to put myself first. "

A new purpose

The gold medallist grew up on the NSW far south coast town of Dalmeny, but moved to Canberra to become a nurse and later a midwife.

Ayers performed as a rower for eight years at an elite level, and first became a Paralympian in 2021, finishing fourth at the Tokyo Games.

Ayers has since moved Adelaide, where her former teammate Jed Altschwager, who retired after Paris in 2024, is also based.

"It's nice to catch up and talk about things that aren't to do with rowing and how we can be better, faster and win that gold," she said.

Nikki Ayers and Jed Altschwager were teammates during the 2024 Paris Paralympics. (ABC News: Brant Cumming)

Although the future is unknown, Ayers said she would maintain her fitness, expressing interest in potentially taking up a different sport.

The Brisbane 2032 Paralympics are in the back of her mind.

"Never say never," she said.

"A lot can happen in six years."

World.title: Football Australia reeling as staff review reveals 'toxic, chaotic' culture
World.content:
The findings of an anonymous survey in which staff complained of working in a "toxic, chaotic and negative" environment will spark internal change at Football Australia (FA), the governing body says.

FA is fighting fires on several fronts, with chief executive Martin Kugeler indicating last week that the organisation would slash 20 per cent of its workforce to rebalance its books.

The cost-cutting measures come as FA prepares to announce a $15.3 million loss at its AGM, following a $8.5 million loss the previous financial year.

Major staff cuts on the horizon as Football Australia posts record loss About 20 per cent of Football Australia staffers face the axe as soccer's governing body posts record losses that doubled last financial year's numbers.

Three of the six directors nominated for Thursday's board elections, including ex-Socceroos goalkeeper Mark Schwarzer, have withdrawn from the running.

The three remaining candidates are all nominated by Australian Professional Leagues (APL) clubs.

But the governing body's culture has also been the subject of intense internal scrutiny, with AAP privy to feedback of a review carried out by consultancy firm Wingmaven in October last year.

Kugeler did not take charge at FA until January this year, and at the time of the internal probe, Heather Garriock, who is currently the organisation's deputy chief executive, was acting interim chief executive.

As part of the survey, staff were asked to select "three words to describe the culture at Football Australia".

Mark Schwarzer is one of three directors who have pulled out of the board elections. (Getty: Mark Kolbe)

According to Wingmaven, feedback, which was delivered to staff in November and has been seen by AAP, more than 70 per cent of the 39 respondents had "overwhelmingly negative" word associations with working at FA.

Staff were shown a word cloud that summed up their responses, and among the terms used to describe working at FA were adjectives such as "hierarchical, bureaucratic and egotistical".

It also highlighted a "toxic, chaotic, gruelling and unprofessional" culture.

Further feedback seen by AAP shows staff indicated that there was a "perceived favouritism" within the organisation and that FA was a workplace with "low psychological safety and trust".

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Additional concerns relayed by staff indicated that there were "meetings about meetings", that decisions were "made on opinion not evidence", and there was an "avoidance culture".

Workers also raised the issue of a divide between staff in Sydney and Melbourne.

FA said in a statement it had taken staff concerns on board and was working to build "positive workplace behaviours" under Kugeler.

"In 2025, Football Australia engaged Wingmaven to examine the culture and performance standards across the commercial, marketing, communications, digital, and events functions," an FA spokesperson said.

"The findings and recommendations have informed organisational changes which have commenced and will continue as part of our organisational restructure.

"Improving culture standards was a key criteria in our search for a new CEO.

"The appointment of Martin Kugeler, who has a proven track record in building high-performance, values-driven cultures, reflects our commitment to strengthening and sustaining positive workplace behaviours."

AAP

World.title: Magnussen flops at Enhanced Games, finishes last twice
World.content:
James Magnussen's first foray into the contentious Enhanced Games has ended in disappointment, with the doped-up Australian Olympian finishing last in the men's 100-metre and 50m freestyle.

Incredibly, the Olympic silver medallist was well beaten in the 100m by American Hunter Armstrong, who entered the event as a "non-enhanced athlete".

Magnussen was also last in the four-man field for the 50m, all of whom were doping, finishing in 21.52 seconds, which is shy of his personal best of 20.98 set 13 years ago.

"Enhanced" Greek swimmer Kristian Gkolomeev won both finals, going 0.07 of a second faster than Australian Cameron McEvoy's legitimate 50m world record of 20.88.

He pocketed US$1 million for the record, the only record of the meet in the final event in the pool.

"We arrived in mainstream culture; we are here to stay," Games CEO Max Martin said.

James Magnussen is taking performance-enhancing drugs. (Getty Images/Enhanced: Greg Doherty)

Earlier, Gkolomeev missed the 100m world record by 0.2 of a second, with non-enhanced Armstrong second in 48.25 seconds.

Ireland's Shane Ryan trailed in third with 48.92 while Magnussen was last, swimming 49.44, more than 2 seconds slower than his own personal best.

The result will be particularly jarring for the 35-year-old Aussie, who was wearing a garish gold super suit, the sort banned by World Aquatics in 2009, in recognition of him being the first athlete to 

Magnussen will likely not be too worried about the time though: even finishing fourth he will pocket $US50,000 ($A70,000).

He will also swim the 50m freestyle at the event.

Athletes can claim a $US1 million bonus for breaking the existing world record at the inaugural Enhanced Games, which are taking place in a purpose-built arena in Las Vegas.

The swimming is taking place in a 50m, four-lane pool.

The concept of the Enhanced Games is that athletes can take performance-enhancing drugs including testosterone, EPO and human growth hormone.

Track and field sprinting and weightlifting are also taking place.

The International Olympic Committee and World Anti-Doping Agency have called the concept a dangerous "betrayal" of sports integrity.

World.title: Did the Giants just end the Lions' AFL premiership hopes?
World.content:
If football is at its most serious in September, it might be at its most routine in May. Finals hopes are rarely made or dashed this early in the year.

While every game of football is important, the long stretch before the bye rounds often sees complacency creep in to fans and clubs alike.

Despite this, yesterday's was an unusually consequential game for this time of year. Brisbane, the two-time defending premiers, had put in one good and one sub-par half in their loss the week before to Geelong.

That capitulation underlined a less-than-stellar run of form for the pacesetters of the competition. Instead of sitting towards the top of the ladder the Lions came into round 11 at the edge of the top six and drifting closer to the edge of the 10.

On the other side of the country, the orange team faced a similar second-half fade-out but to a far inferior opponent. GWS's loss to the Eagles in Perth was yet another confusing step for a team struggling to find its groove.

Giants vs Lions, Bulldogs vs Demons Greater Western Sydney has left reigning premier Brisbane reeling with a record-breaking goal surge, while the Bulldogs get home in a see-sawing contest against the Demons.

While the Lions were trying to catch up to the ladder leaders, the Giants were faced with the task of staying in touch with the bottom of the top 10.

Both sides needed a win to solidify how they were playing, more than to save their finals hopes.

Early on, the game seemed poised to be a tight battle between two teams trying to right the ship. The lead oscillated, with just a kick in it at half-time. Partisan fans in the crowd would have been chomping on nails, while neutrals at home set themselves for yet another Sunday afternoon classic.

The second half certainly delivered one of the most memorable outcomes in recent years, just not the close game that the first half promised.

It took just 27 seconds for Phoenix Gothard to slot the Giants' first for the quarter, and Jake Stringer spent about a minute and three quarters adding another. In the next 35 minutes, the Giants added a dozen more majors in a scintillating display seen once in a generation at best.

"That was unbelievable, that third quarter. That was probably the funnest period of a game I've had in my life. So good!" Gothard said after the game.

"Our backs were elite. Our forwards were elite. Our mids were elite. Everything clicked."

The quarter entered the record books as equal-fourth-biggest scoring term in history, the biggest in fifteen years, and the biggest ever against a reigning premier.

So how did the Giants pull off their dramatic surge and how serious is the trouble up at the Lions' den?

How the Giants did the damage

Giants small forwards like Brent Daniels were too fast, too fierce and too quick to pick up on errors by the Lions. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Cameron Spencer)

When looking at how a team dismantles another, the first port of call is usually its strengths, or the opposition's weaknesses. Football matches are often a battle between styles and preferred "brands" of play.

Coming into the game, GWS has arguably been the strongest side at scoring from their defensive half over the past three seasons, and Brisbane has struggled to defend there, conceding the second-most points per game from their defensive half.

In a press conference in the days before the match, Brisbane coach Chris Fagan talked about his team's struggles.

"Our team defence has been inconsistent," he said.

"We've been scored against a lot from our front half. So we've been looking at why we've been inconsistent with that."

Given all of that, one would expect that a large portion of that monstrous 85-point thumping would have been generated from the Giants defensive end. Instead, it was the front half where much of the damage was done.

The Giants' potent small forward brigade pressured the Lions into uncharacteristic mistakes and unfavourable situations. The Giants have had a revolving door in their forward half this year, with little continuity from week to week.

Against the Lions, talismanic key forward Jesse Hogan was out of action, leaving GWS with yet another forward line. Only Gothard has played every game predominantly up forward, with a host of other options rotating for stretches around the youngster.

The combination on Sunday might have sparked something magical, at least for a quarter.

The Lions have one of the clearest methods for ball movement in the league. They have long been the league's best team at controlling tempo through uncontested marks.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Pressuring the kicker across the whole field and preventing open outlets is critical for disrupting the Lions' game. So far this year, the Lions are averaging 79 kicks to uncontested marks per game. On Sunday, the Giants limited the Lions to just 57 all day, including a miserly six in the third quarter.

"Our pressure was great. We restricted their uncontested marks, which was our game plan." Gothard said.

The Lions managed only one inside 50 when starting from their defensive half in the third term, and moved it past halfway just four times in the period. Ordinarily, the Lions are one of the best four teams at moving the ball from defensive 50 to their attacking 50. Their rate in the third would have been the worst for any side.

The Lions' decision-making in the quarter was uncharacteristically erratic through the onslaught, with part of the frustration from an inability to win the ball in the contest. This lack of first-use ball may have factored into Lions players being more aggressive with their ball use than usual.

Losing that first opportunity is something that Brisbane doesn't usually have to deal with.

Coming into the game, the Lions led the league in clearance differential both in the centre and around the ground. But the Giants are the league's strongest team at winning ground balls, particularly ground balls that happen after clearances.

While the Giants only narrowly won the clearance battle in the third quarter, they controlled the ball whenever it hit the deck, pouncing on loose moments and half chances.

"When you can't win the footy and you can't get possession of it, this game's pretty hard to play. And that's been the pattern for the last three weeks in third quarters. We've just been beaten in the contest and in the clearance," Fagan said post-game.

The numbers seem to back up Fagan's frank assessment. Over the last month, Brisbane has conceded more points from clearances in the third quarter than the entire first half combined. This is a relatively small sample, but deciding whether to identify and address such microtrends is nuts-and-bolts coaching.

But a large amount of credit needs to go to the Giants, who seem to prepare better for teams that like to retain possession via the marking game than most other sides.

The straightest kicking ever?

The method of how they prompted the surge only explains a part of that record-breaking score. The bigger part was how they actually put the 14 majors on the board.

If the saying that "good kicking is good football" is accurate then there may have never been better football than for those 37-odd minutes yesterday afternoon.

"The third quarter just felt like everything we touched turned to gold. So that's nice when it happens. It doesn't happen often, obviously." GWS coach Adam Kingsley said after the game.

The Giants' third quarter was one of the most extreme examples of a side simply unable to miss. From set shots to falling snaps, GWS took (almost) every opportunity it was given. Gothard and Toby Greene even managed to snap goals on each foot in the quarter.

The Giants onslaught was the most accurate goalkicking performance for at least the past decade when adjusting for the difficulty of the shots taken. The Giants would ordinarily be expected to kick just eight of their 14 goals.

That sort of accuracy isn't just unusual — it's a historical over-performance. Prior to this game the best quarter for accuracy at volume was Geelong's run in the 2017 Easter Monday game when the Cats drilled 10 straight to sink Hawthorn.

Of those 10 majors, the Cats would have been expected to kick about six goals. On Sunday, GWS beat Geelong's mark by half again.

Seemingly every lucky bounce of the ball or gust of wind went the Giants' way in the quarter — and against the will of the Lions. As the quarter progressed, the Lions players seemingly went from dumbfounded to dejected by the Giants' unerring ability to find the gap between the big sticks.

It's unlikely the Giants — or any team — will be able to repeat the display anytime soon. That doesn't make it any less powerful, but a marker of how utterly unbelievable their surge was.

Will the Lions be alright?

Coach Chris Fagan, skipper Harris Andrews and the Lions have had bad losses to the Giants before - in 2024, they rebounded to win the flag. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Mark Metcalfe)

Already, questions have started to turn to the legitimacy of the Lions' finals hopes, autumn football be damned. Perhaps the most important person didn't immediately overreact to the loss, and with some good historical reasons.

"I take a little bit of heart from the fact that a couple of years ago the Giants beat us up in a similar fashion in Canberra and we got written off," Fagan said.

That loss two years ago dropped the Lions to two wins from just seven games and 13th on the ladder. Of course, they were on top of the footballing world by the last Saturday in September.

"Fair enough. We should get written off tonight, too," Fagan said.

"But we're able to respond to that (performance) and make finals and go on and win a premiership [like in 2024]. So, this is one moment in time."

History also tells us that such a bad quarter and loss isn't a disqualifying feature for an eventual premier.

Often forgotten in the glow of premiership glory is that most years feature ups and downs. No team goes undefeated (unless they are the North Melbourne AFLW team) and quite often even the premiers have copped big losses en route to September. This includes games where they just couldn't stop opponents running rampant.

Sometimes, a flag involves a bit of revenge for one of these bad days.

The team that unexpectedly gets the premier's number is often not a top side, with plenty of lowly teams claiming a scalp that looks baffling in hindsight.

Chris Fagan and his Lions get their fairytale ending at the MCG Twelve months on from a devastating loss at the MCG, coach Chris Fagan and his Lions deliver the perfect send-off to a rollercoaster season that could have been the script of a glossy TV drama.

While all this history provides some comfort for Lions fans, it doesn't detract from the dip in form that Brisbane has suffered in recent weeks. Fagan isn't shirking away from the fact the Lions need to improve if they are to complete the threepeat.

"It's not a great moment," he said. "It's not the highlight of my coaching career here at the Brisbane Lions, I can assure you of that.

"But it is a moment that we can sort of choose whether we get better from it or we continue to go backwards. Because at the moment we're going backwards and we're nowhere near a premiership fancy at all."

The Lions have come back from here once before and time will tell if they can do it again.
